passages.section: Radio-to-Pose Information for Gauge-Drift Correction in Cooperative Localization
passages.location: Radio-to-Pose Information for Gauge-Drift Correction in Cooperative Localization
passages.text: Cooperative localization uses odometry and inter-robot measurements to estimate the motion of a robot team. These measurements describe only relative geometry, but the team’s estimated position and orientation can drift together over time, i.e. , gauge drift . In this work, we study correction of this gauge drift using a radio attenuation map registered in the same world coordinate frame used for robot poses. Specifically, we propose Radio-to-Pose Information (RPI), an interface that converts power residuals and their pose derivatives into a Gaussian information matrix and vector pair. RPI builds on the insight that received power is sensitive to shared displacement in the world map. The pose estimator uses the interface together with odometry and inter-robot measurements to update poses and minimize uncertainty. We characterize the shared motions detectable from the map and observed links. For an uncertain shared map, RPI keeps correlations across robots and time and reproduces joint Gaussian pose estimates and covariances. Across 1000 1000 simulated Gaussian trials, RPI matches the results of joint estimation. Across 32 paired trials with a registered map, RPI reduces common-position RMSE from 0.542 0.542 m to 0.140 0.140 m in a 50 × 50 50\times 50 m arena compared with a baseline that uses radio only to weight relative measurements.

To carry out tasks such as exploration, mapping, and environmental monitoring, robot teams rely on coordinated motion and shared observations. When global positioning is unavailable, they can estimate motion through odometry and inter-robot measurements. These observations constrain relative geometry, but the estimated team can move away from its true location as a group. For example, translating every robot estimate by one meter leaves all pairwise distances unchanged. This shared error matters when robots must reach mapped destinations or report observations in world coordinates.

It is also important to precisely estimate uncertainty because the team can know its relative geometry while remaining uncertain about its position in the world. This ambiguity is called gauge freedom . Gauge freedom describes indistinguishable coordinate frames, which in the presence of motion or noise leads to gauge drift . Gauge drift describes the temporal growth of error or uncertainty in these shared-motion directions. Teams construct a reference frame from a prior over their initial poses, but subsequent noisy observations determine how well the team remains localized. For trajectories without a fixed point of reference, common translations and rotations maintain relative observations, but they do not provide useful information about global state.

A radio attenuation map aligned to the world frame can provide a reference because received power depends on both link length and the attenuation field. For example, in Fig. 1 , a common translation preserves separation and distance loss but changes link attenuation. Using a global attenuation map which captures knowledge of obstacles in the environment can help distinguish the team’s positions by using differences in the received power they observe.

Fig. 1: In the left map, when there is no registered attenuation map, equal-length links have identical distance-only predictions. In the right map, when a registered map is present, equal-length links have different power predictions. Colors indicate attenuation in dB/m.

We propose the Radio-to-Pose Information (RPI) interface which leverages this behavior. The RPI is an interface between two components: First, a radio module predicts received power from the current poses and attenuation map, then determines the power mismatch and pose sensitivity as an information matrix and vector. Second, a pose estimator uses this message to compute a correction and its uncertainty.
This paper describes three contributions:
We show that fixed weights on relative measurements add zero direct information about common motion. We characterize which shared motions the attenuation map and observed links can detect.
We propose the Radio-to-Pose Information (RPI) interface, which converts power residuals and pose sensitivity into an information matrix and vector for pose estimation.

We derive centroid covariance growth and a lower bound on mean-squared common-position error under stated motion and measurement assumptions. We evaluate agreement with joint estimation, drift correction, and sensitivity to map error.

Cooperative Localization. Relative measurements help robots estimate their positions with respect to one another, but they do not determine the position and orientation of the entire team in the world frame [ 1 , 2 ] . Gauge fixing chooses a coordinate frame for estimation [ 3 ] . Simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) adds persistent environmental features and loop closures, which can reduce trajectory drift [ 4 ] . However, a map built only from the robot’s own measurements defines position relative to the robot’s chosen coordinate frame rather than an externally registered world frame. Our comparison concerns a cooperative localizer that uses radio to set fixed weights on relative factors.

Radio and Field Maps. Radio tomography estimates spatial attenuation from power measurements and known link positions [ 5 ] . Radio SLAM jointly estimates motion and propagation structure using radio observations, including multipath information [ 6 , 7 ] . Its reference frame depends on the available anchors and priors. Known physical anchors can provide a reference [ 7 ] , but may not be available. Instead, this paper focuses on studying inter-robot links against a registered attenuation field. This follows the principle of localization against surveyed terrain or magnetic maps [ 8 , 9 ] .

Gaussian Fusion. Factor-graph smoothers combine measurement models and priors through local linearization [ 4 ] . Gaussian elimination provides a way to summarize part of this model for another estimator. Distributed smoothing must account for previously shared information when summaries are replaced [ 10 ] . Fusion with shared variables must also preserve the induced correlations or use an appropriate conservative approximation [ 11 , 12 ] . RPI applies these requirements to a radio module whose uncertain map is shared across robots and time. Equivalent radio factors in a factor-graph smoother give the same local Gaussian result when the models and linearizations agree.

If gauge drift occurs, the robot team’s collective position (i.e., the centroid) relative to the world map becomes uncertain (§ IV-A ). We show that while existing techniques based on relative measurements alone cannot solve the gauge drift problem for robot teams (§ IV-B ), it is possible to use radio field attenuation information from the world map to reduce this source of error (§ IV-C ).

The proposition shows that fixed-weight relative measurements provide no direct information about shared translation or rotation. Additional pose information can come from modeling how received radio power depends on the robot poses.

A registered attenuation map can constrain this common motion when shared displacement changes the power predicted for the observed links. Radio sensitivity to shared motion depends on how that motion changes the attenuation sampled by the observed links. Because a shared rigid motion leaves link length unchanged, only the map attenuation term changes the predicted power.

With the map fixed and link weights satisfying w ℓ ​ ( g ​ v , g ​ X ) = w ℓ ​ ( v , X ) w_{\ell}(gv,gX)=w_{\ell}(v,X) , we use Eq. ( 2 ) to construct several simple examples of unresolved motion. A constant field has zero spatial gradient, so the radio model cannot detect any shared translation or rotation. If F ⁡ ( v ) = f ⁡ ( v x ) F(v)=f(v_{x}) , vertical translation does not change sampled link attenuation. A radial field cannot distinguish rotation about its center. Uncertain field values reduce the information carried by these derivatives. Repeated map patterns can produce the same radio measurements at different team locations. However, the full rank of the shared-motion Jacobian ensures local distinguishability. This means that any small shared translation or rotation of the team changes at least one predicted radio measurement.

We design RPI using the insight that a radio map aligned to world coordinates can provide a reference for the team’s position. We treat the map’s position and orientation in world coordinates as known. This method accounts for Gaussian uncertainty in its attenuation values as we describe in § V-B . We introduce RPI to pass information from the radio module to the pose estimator, as Fig. 3 illustrates.

Uncertainty in the shared map can affect pose estimates for multiple robots at different times. RPI therefore combines the radio measurements across robots and time steps before eliminating the map variables. This maintains the cross-robot and cross-time correlations the shared map induces. With respect to Proposition 3 , the resulting message gives the exact pose marginal for the Gaussian system.

The pose estimator reconstructs the RPI interface after each relinearization. For N N robots and L L time steps, a pose information matrix requires O ⁡ ( N 2 ​ L 2 ) O(N^{2}L^{2}) storage. The RPI message contains ( Λ , η ) (\Lambda,\eta) , the order of the pose variables, and the linearization point.

Fig. 5 shows that fixed-map RPI and Joint overlap, with final-third common-position RMSE of 0.981 0.981 , 0.659 0.659 , and 1.183 1.183 m under registration, attenuation, and combined errors, respectively. Uncertain-map RPI reduces these errors to 0.957 0.957 , 0.172 0.172 , and 0.967 0.967 m, while maintaining relative RMSE near 0.060 0.060 m, and outperforms Scalar’s 0.542 0.542 m under attenuation error, but not under registration or combined errors. In this work, we showed how a registered attenuation map provides information about shared robot motion that fixed weights on relative measurements cannot directly supply. We introduced RPI, a mathematical interface that converts radio measurements and map information into pose information while preserving shared-map correlations. Our analysis characterizes which shared motions the map and observed links can detect.

Our simulations confirm that RPI matches the pose estimates and covariances from the benchmarked joint optimization method. Our nonlinear experiments show reduced common-position error while maintaining relative-position accuracy, with directional map ablations confirming that correction occurs in map-constrained directions. Map mismatch can increase position error without a corresponding increase in reported uncertainty. Future work will evaluate RPI on real measured radio data and study pose-update convergence. We will release the code upon acceptance.
